tldr: RET-LLM equips LLMs with a scalable, updatable, interpretable, and aggregatable external memory unit that stores knowledge as triplets, enabling explicit read-write operations for improved question answering, especially on temporal facts.
contributions: A novel RET-LLM framework with a triplet-based memory unit inspired by Davidsonian semantics
A text-based Memory-API enabling LLMs to generate read/write calls to an external memory
Fine-tuning of Alpaca-7B using LoRA on synthetic data to learn memory API invocation
Demonstration of superior performance over baselines in QA, including temporal question answering
methods: The RET-LLM framework consists of three components: a fine-tuned LLM (Alpaca-7B with LoRA), a controller, and a triplet-based memory unit. The LLM is fine-tuned on synthetic datasets encoding relationships between people and organizations to learn generating memory API calls (MEM_WRITE and MEM_READ). Knowledge is extracted and stored as triplets in a three-column table, with average vector representations also stored in a Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH) table for fuzzy search. During retrieval, the system first attempts exact match lookups, then falls back to LSH-based vector similarity search.
results: Qualitative evaluations demonstrate that RET-LLM outperforms baseline approaches like Alpaca-7B in question answering tasks. In zero-shot evaluations, Alpaca-7B produced incorrect answers even when all required information was present in the context, while RET-LLM stored extracted triplets and answered correctly without reinputting the context. The framework also handled temporal-based QA tasks effectively, such as tracking changing facts like US presidency, which standard LLMs struggle with due to static training data.
limitations: Evaluation is primarily qualitative rather than quantitative
The synthetic dataset used for fine-tuning is limited in scope (single domain of people-relationship-organizations)
LSH-based retrieval may not always find a match, resulting in empty query outputs
No large-scale benchmarking across diverse domains is presented
